item.title: Reclaiming nature’s many delights through living fences [Book Review]
item.dc:creator: Usha Rai
item.author: Renuka Kulkarni
item.topic-tags: Biodiversity, Cities and Towns, Plantations, Plants, and Trees
item.description:
- Planted hedges have been integral to the landscape in India and around the world, but have been changed and reduced due to urbanisation.
- The book The Living Fence is a guide to all those who yearn for the peace and beauty of green spaces, and who’d like to build small biodiversity refuges in their compound walls.
- Based on five years of travel and research by landscape architect Sonali Dahotre, the book is a collection of photographs, field observations, and ecological notes on over 250 plant species in India, highlighting their ecological roles and their potential in supporting biodiversity.
item.content:encoded: My neighbour in Gurugram has a hedge of roses and jasmines outside the brick wall of her house. Just before the rains it is fragrant with white jasmines and in the winter season there are clusters of small pink and white roses on the hedge. My house, also in Gurugram, has a hedgerow of hibiscus trees outside a brick and grill fencing. The trees are uneven and in the flowering season, which is almost round the year, there are red, orange and pink hibiscus flowers. Both the hedge and the hedgerow attract squirrels, butterflies and birds. I have seen bulbuls nesting in the thickest parts of the hedgerow. In the hot summer months, many people put earthen pots of water for birds and squirrels adjacent to the fencing or in courtyards. There were also chameleons, before Gurugram became highly urbanised. During the rainy season, I have also seen many snakes in the undergrowth. A few months ago, I spotted one in the tree fencing that separates my house and my sister’s. The adjoining tall and stately kanak champa (Pterospermum acerifolium) also in the fenced area, is home to many birds and bees, the latter occasionally building their honeycombs in them or the adjoining tall trees. These fences, teeming with life, still exist at a time when floods, climate change and the rampant growth of brick and concrete buildings and industrial hubs are decimating our rural and urban landscapes and eating into the spaces of birds, bees and a myriad other creatures…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.title: Ganges river dolphins may synchronise their activity with time, tides and the moon
item.dc:creator: Sneha Mahale
item.author: Priyanka Shankar
item.topic-tags: Animal Behaviour, Biodiversity, Conservation, Ecology, Endangered species, Endemic species, Mammals, Rivers, and Wildlife
item.description:
- A new month-long study used underwater acoustic recordings to study Ganges river dolphins in West Bengal’s Rupnarayan river.
- Dolphin detections peaked at dawn and dusk. Tidal height showed a stronger relationship than the time and lunar cycle.
- While the study covered only one lunar cycle and did not measure prey availability, the findings could help improve dolphin surveys by incorporating more drivers in monitoring.
item.content:encoded: In the tidal waters of West Bengal’s Rupnarayan river, Ganges river dolphins live with constantly shifting water levels, currents and conditions. A new study in the river found that tide, time of day and lunar cycle influences when the dolphins were detected. Published in Aquatic Mammals, the month-long study examined the these parameters together in relation to acoustic detections (monitoring the animal by the sounds it makes) of Ganges river dolphins. At the study site, tides rise and fall twice a day with occasional tidal bores, causing large shifts in water levels and the currents, explains Gargi Roy Chowdhury, principal project associate at Wildlife Institute of India (WII) and the first author of the study. “It is a human-modified landscape with intense motorised fishing, and industrialised lower reaches with the Kolaghat thermal power plant downstream of the study site. It holds a good population of dolphins,” she adds while noting that large vessel traffic is limited here. A river shaped by the tide The Rupnarayan is an 85-km-long tributary of the Hooghly, influenced by tides from the Bay of Bengal, about 220 km away. Its upper reaches have narrower channels, while the lower stretches are wider. The river also experiences periodic tidal bores, and its flow is shaped by both seasonal and tidal forces. item.title: As El Niño strengthens, coral reefs face narrow windows for recovery
item.dc:creator: Max Martin
item.author: Kundan Pandey
item.topic-tags: Biodiversity, Coast, Conservation, Coral Reefs, Ecology, Environment, Extreme Weather Events, Fish, Global Warming, and Oceans
item.description:
- Repeated marine heatwaves are hitting reefs before they can fully recover, raising the risk of long-term decline.
- Since 1998, every strong El Niño has coincided with a global coral bleaching event, and each event has affected more reef areas than the last.
- Indian reefs show sharply different responses across regions, highlighting the role of local conditions and the need for sustained monitoring of the 2026–27 El Niño.
item.content:encoded: As UN Secretary-General António Guterres says, El Niño is being “supersized” by a warming climate. The UN Environment Programme (UNEP) warns that coral reefs are being hit by new bleaching events before they have had time to recover from earlier ones. UNEP likened reefs to “an overmatched boxer” taking repeated blows, citing findings from the Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network (GCRMN) of the International Coral Reef Initiative (ICRI). The outlook is stark. “Multiple lines of evidence indicate that the majority (70-90%) of warm water (tropical) coral reefs that exist today will disappear even if global warming is constrained to 1.5°C,” as the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change warns. The headline, however, is that marine heatwaves are narrowing the window for coral reef recovery. “Coral reefs once had decades to recover after major bleaching events. Today, they’re lucky to get five or six years,” said Manuel González Rivero, a reef expert at The Australian Institute of Marine Science and lead author of the GCRMN report. “And for many reefs affected by the unprecedented marine heatwaves in 2024, this year’s El Niño likely means they’ll have had little more than a year to begin recovering before being hit again.” “India’s own reefs show the same trend,” said marine biologist Amruth P., assistant professor in the Department of Life Sciences at CHRIST University, Bengaluru. “A 24-year study in Lakshadweep recorded coral cover falling from about 37% to under 20% since 1998 after repeated marine heatwaves.” The study by the Mysuru-based Nature Conservation Foundation…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.title: The emotional cost of displacement
item.dc:creator: Arathi M.R.
item.author: Arathimenon
item.topic-tags: Cities and Towns, Climate Change, Coast, Coastal erosion, Environment, Extreme Weather Events, Fishing, Floods, Health impacts, Human Rights, Oceans, People, and Villages
item.description:
- Coastal erosion is creating a prolonged state of displacement and insecurity among the fishing communities in Kerala’s Thiruvananthapuram.
- A study suggests Thiruvananthapuram’s coast has lost over 2.6 sq. km of land to coastal erosion over a 14-year period.
- The government rehabilitation scheme separates community members from each other and their livelihoods leading to social, economic and psychological distress.
item.content:encoded: “This was our home,” says 43-year-old Baby Titus, pointing to a green-painted house secured with a rusty lock. Waves were repeatedly crashing on the right side of the house. “The sea kept entering and receding, and it caused a short circuit inside the house. You would get an electric shock wherever you touched.” A road past Kollamkode Church in Thiruvananthapuram leads to the Arabian Sea, where rows of houses like Titus’s line the shoreline. Many houses here have been engulfed by the sea. The remains of those houses, along with the granite boulders dumped into the sea for a seawall, are constantly battered by the waves, each surge crashing against them with a frightening roar. Kulathoor grama panchayat is the southernmost grama panchayat in Thiruvananthapuram district in Kerala. Its coastal wards, including Pozhipallivilakam, Mullassery, Kollamkode, Paruthiyoor, Pozhikara Beach and Pozhiyoor, have been facing severe coastal erosion for decades. Many of these wards have only seven or eight rows of houses remaining, out of about 100. Of those that remain, only a few are inhabited. Fearing the house was structurally precarious and hence, unsafe, Baby Titus now lives in a rented two-bedroom house next door with her husband and three adolescent children, paying ₹2,000 a month. The house’s owners have moved elsewhere due to flooding. Baby Titus spends the night listening anxiously to the sound of every crashing wave, wondering whether the sea is coming in — a reality shared by the families living along the coast. item.title: Study identifies rare case of moth and lichen association
item.dc:creator: Arathi Menon

item.description: A new paper documents the first known record of a moth using the umbilicate lichen, Lasallia pertusa, as a camouflage background. Published in the journal Arthropod-Plant Interactions, the observation was made in July 2025 at Duggi, in Kugti Wildlife Sanctuary, Chamba district, Himachal Pradesh, at about 3,200 m elevation. Lichen-associated camouflage has been documented before, […]
item.content:encoded: A new paper documents the first known record of a moth using the umbilicate lichen, Lasallia pertusa, as a camouflage background. Published in the journal Arthropod-Plant Interactions, the observation was made in July 2025 at Duggi, in Kugti Wildlife Sanctuary, Chamba district, Himachal Pradesh, at about 3,200 m elevation. Lichen-associated camouflage has been documented before, including in moths. In this case, however, the association involves an umbilicate (attached to its substrate only at a single point), foliose (with flat, leaf-like lobes) lichen, rather than the more commonly documented crustose or bark-growing lichens. The finding, therefore, expands the range of lichen growth forms known to potentially participate in insect camouflage. It also points to the fact that a seemingly inconspicuous lichen can be an important part of an animal’s visual environment and survival strategy. One of the authors, Sanjay Kumar Uniyal, informs Mongabay-India that though there have been similar observations of moths mimicking lichens in the past, this particular lichen species has been documented for the first time. “This might have an evolutionary consequence which can only be understood through further studies,” Unniyal shares. L. pertusa has a large, perforated and highly irregular thallus (vegetative body), providing a particularly complex visual background, reports the paper. The moth that belongs to the family Noctuidae, was found resting directly on the lichen growing on exposed rock. The moth’s identification was based on photographs and expert examination. The paper reports that the moth species couldn’t be identified due to the absence of a specimen.…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.content:encoded: India is promoting deep-sea fishing with the promise of better incomes for the country’s traditional fishers. Government schemes have sought to accelerate this transition by providing financial support for deep-sea fishing vessels. Yet the move into deeper waters has proved far more complicated than policy documents suggest. Across the coastal states of India, fishing communities are raising concerns about whether the economics of deep-sea fishing are actually feasible for India’s fishers. In several major fishing states, the government-backed schemes to promote deep-sea fishing have struggled to attract takers. This series follows the 2020-2025 phase of India’s deep sea fishing scheme and examines the country’s ambitions, the boats designed to make it possible, the growing focus on high-value species, and, most importantly, the realities faced by fishers being asked to invest in an uncertain future. Through months of field reporting and conversations with communities across India’s coastal states, Right to Information replies and Lok Sabha reports, Mongabay-India examines what it will take to keep India’s deep sea dreams afloat. This series was produced in partnership with the Pulitzer Center’s Ocean Reporting Network.This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.title: India’s deep-sea fishing dreams are struggling to stay afloat
item.dc:creator: Supriya Vohra
item.author: Aditi Tandon
item.description:
- India’s deep-sea fishing scheme has few takers as high costs, unsuitable boat designs and delayed subsidies deter participation.
- The government approved 392 deep-sea fishing vessels under the scheme’s 2020–25 implementation period. But so far, fewer than half of the approved boats have actually been ordered.
- Despite these challenges, India is expanding its deep-sea and high-seas fishing ambitions, with new policies and programmes focused on tuna and other high-value species.
- Through field reporting, RTI replies and Lok Sabha reports, Mongabay-India reviewed the status of the five-year scheme and found gaps between policy and reality.
item.content:encoded: This story is the first in a series on deep-sea fishing in India, produced in partnership with the Pulitzer Center’s Ocean Reporting Network. The first story examines India’s Deep Sea Fishing Vessel Scheme and finds a mismatch between its ambitions and the realities of fishing. Shaju Antony, a traditional fisherman from Kerala, was encouraged by his parish priest to apply for a government scheme in 2020 that provided financial assistance for deep-sea fishing vessels. He gathered about ₹7.2 million for his part of the contribution for a boat under the Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada Yojana (PMMSY), a central government scheme. He received the boat three years later, in December 2023. But the boat started showing signs of trouble as soon as he started using it. Antony and his crew spent another ₹3 million repairing the boat. Finally, after months of sending petitions to the state government to look into the matter, he gave up. “If they are building boats for fishermen, why aren’t they consulting the fishermen?” he asks. About 1500 km further up, on the west coast of India, Kiran Koli, a traditional fisherman and leader of a fishers’ union from Maharashtra, had also applied for the same government scheme in 2017-18 when it was under the government’s Neel Kranti (Blue Revolution) Mission. In 2020, when the scheme became Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada Yojana, Koli was the first person on the list, he says. In June 2026, nearly a decade after he first applied, Koli received his boat. item.title: A changing climate is reshaping India’s infectious disease risks
item.dc:creator: Rupsy Khurana
item.author: Priyanka Shankar
item.topic-tags: Cities and Towns, Climate Change, Climate Change Adaptation, Climate Science, Drought, Environment, Extreme Weather Events, Floods, Global Warming, Health impacts, Human Rights, and Impacts of Climate Change
item.description:
- Heatwaves, floods, erratic rainfall and droughts are altering the conditions that drive infectious diseases.
- Poorly managed drainage, sewage and water infrastructure can amplify health risks during extreme weather.
- India is working on climate-health surveillance and early-warning systems, but gaps in data and infrastructure could limit its ability to predict and prevent outbreaks, experts say.
item.content:encoded: When extreme weather events occur, the damage is usually measured in collapsed buildings, damaged roads and flooded homes. But the aftermath also brings a less visible threat. Heatwaves, droughts, erratic rainfall and flash floods, in combination or alone, also reshape the ecology of diseases. They can affect how long pathogens survive, change the distribution of disease-carrying insects and bring people, animals and pathogens into closer contact, increasing the risk of outbreaks in new places at unexpected times. The latest assessment report by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change has warned that heatwaves and extreme rainfall events are projected to increase in the coming years. A 2025 study by IPE Global, an international development consultancy, and Esri India, a GIS mapping company, warns that extreme weather could become more severe by 2030, with heatwaves projected to double in major cities and extreme rainfall events expected to rise by 43% across the country. Health experts state that we need to factor in and prevent climate-related outbreaks rather than simply responding to them. Health risks during monsoons and droughts The World Meteorological Organisation (WMO) reports that the past decade has witnessed some of the worst floods on record. India, too, has experienced devastating floods, including those in Mumbai in 2025 and Kerala in 2018. “Heavy rainfall and flooding create ideal conditions for the emergence and spread of infections,” shares Surya Prasad, a consultant physician at Manipal Hospital, Bengaluru. “Floodwater overwhelms sewage systems and mixes human and animal waste into water sources, while warmer…This article was originally published on Mongabay

The species had once been wiped out from the park but was brought back through wild-to-wild translocation and rhino rehabilitation programmes. A recent study of the re-established population offers encouraging signs of adaptation in its restored habitat. The greater one-horned rhino (Rhinoceros […]
item.content:encoded: Conservation efforts have re-established the greater one-horned rhinoceros in Assam’s Manas National Park. The species had once been wiped out from the park but was brought back through wild-to-wild translocation and rhino rehabilitation programmes. A recent study of the re-established population offers encouraging signs of adaptation in its restored habitat. The greater one-horned rhino (Rhinoceros unicornis) is the largest of the three rhino species found in Asia. It is identified by a single black horn, about 8-25 inches long, and grey-brown hide with skin folds that give it an armour-plated appearance. It’s about half the weight of an elephant, going up to 2,700 kilograms and is around 6.5 feet tall. Despite its size, the rhino is a good swimmer and spends considerable time in wetlands and grasslands. It mainly feeds on grasses, leaves, branches of shrubs and trees, fruit, and aquatic plants. The greater one-horned rhino now numbers at around 4,075 individuals found only in the grasslands of India and Nepal. The IUCN Red List classifies the species as vulnerable, which means it faces a high risk of extinction in the wild. In India, it receives the highest legal protection under Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, and is listed in Appendix I of CITES, which bans international trade. Rhinos play an important role in shaping grassland and wetland ecosystems. However, habitat loss and fragmentation, invasive species and human-animal conflict remain major threats to the species. The rhino has also faced illegal hunting for its horns. In a…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.title: Humid heat challenges India’s conventional heatwave thresholds
item.dc:creator: Barasha Das
item.author: Aditi Tandon
item.description:
- Assam rarely crosses IMD’s heatwave thresholds, despite a measurable warming trend and more frequent spells of anomalous heat.
- Experts say that wet-bulb temperature, which accounts for humidity, may better capture Assam’s heat stress than the dry-bulb temperature used in current heatwave criteria.
- Heat risk varies across Assam’s six agro-climatic zones and district-level vulnerability profiles, pointing to the need for localised heat plans rather than a single uniform state-level plan.
item.content:encoded: Every summer, as Central and Northwest India temperatures rise above 45°C,  the India Meteorological Department (IMD) issues heatwave alerts. Assam, in the northeast, rarely appears on the national heat map, despite high temperatures recorded across the state. Across Assam, several stations have recorded maximum temperatures above 37°C and, in some instances, reached or exceeded 40°C in recent years. In September 2023, Guwahati recorded  38.2°C, 6.4°C above normal, while Silchar recorded 39.4°C, 7.4°C above normal. On May 25, 2024, Guwahati recorded 40.1°C,  at least 8°C above normal. Later that year, the city recorded 39.3°C in September, breaking its all-time temperature record for the month. More recently, in July, maximum temperatures in Guwahati, Dibrugarh, Tezpur and Dhubri were around 4-5°C above normal for which the IMD issued a rare yellow alert. These recordings highlight a challenge Assam continues to face: temperatures that do not always meet India’s conventional heatwave criteria can still produce significant heat stress. Urban heat assessments of the state’s three major cities between 2020 and 2025 by the Directorate of Town and Country Planning show that land-use change, shrinking water bodies, loss of greenery and unplanned development are altering the cities’ thermal landscapes. Guwahati’s heat islands are expanding into larger heat corridors. Dibrugarh is seeing intensifying heat in its densely built core, while Silchar is emerging as the fastest-warming urban centre, with a sharp rise in critical heat-risk zones. Recent district-level precautionary advisories have included  school closures or revised timings and restrictions on outdoor activities. Guwahati, Assam. item.title: Forgotten vegetables could help make our diets more resilient
item.dc:creator: Sharmila Vaidyanathan
item.author: Priyanka Shankar
item.description:
- Vegetable biodiversity is important for nutritional security and climate resilience, but it is rapidly declining due to diet homogenisation and land-use change.
- A global database lists 1,482 vegetable species, although researchers warn that the actual number is much higher, considering regional and local biodiversity.
- There are ongoing efforts in India to protect heirloom vegetables and introduce underutilised vegetables in school meals.
- Meanwhile experts emphasise that conserving vegetable species in national and international gene banks is vital.
item.content:encoded: The clove bean is fondly known as mookuthi avarai in Tamil, an ode to its nose-pin-like appearance. Clove bean belongs to the same family as the morning glory, perennial fast-growing vines that are known for their brightly coloured flowers, and is not a true bean species. Once a common vegetable in south Indian kitchens, clove bean now remains immortalised in S. Meenakshi Ammal’s iconic cookbook Samaithu Paar (Cook and See in Tamil), first published in 1951. Today, clove beans are a rare, if not impossible sight in vegetable markets and seem to have completely disappeared from India’s culinary landscape. However, in one small farm in Bengaluru, landscape architect, natural farmer and founder of Hariyalee Seeds, Prabhakar Rao, continues to conserve the seeds of this and other long-forgotten vegetables. As Rao walks around his farm’s undulating land, pointing to heirloom vegetables like the Yerengere white long eggplant or various tomato varieties, he laments how vegetable markets today are dominated by hybrids. There was a time when the Yerengere white long eggplant was the only brinjal variety that went into the making of vangi bath or brinjal rice, says Rao. “People are all eating the same few vegetables, and the loss of vegetable biodiversity has not received a lot of attention. Why would it? Every vegetable that you use at home is available in abundance,” says Rao. Yerengere white long eggplant at Prabhakar Rao’s farm. Image by Sharmila Vaidyanathan. item.title: India needs a just adaptation agenda [Commentary]
item.dc:creator: Ishan KukretiSarada Prasanna DasSony R K
item.author: Kundan Pandey
item.description:
- India’s first National Adaptation Plan offers an opportunity to make justice central to how the country addresses climate risks and allocates public resources.
- Decisions about whose risks receive attention and who benefits from interventions can reinforce existing inequalities, so adaptation must be just.
- A just adaptation agenda requires enforceable commitments to community participation, vulnerability-based funding, grievance redress and independent monitoring of who benefits.
- The views in this commentary are those of the authors.
item.content:encoded: Climate impacts in India are becoming increasingly visible. As parts of the country, including Assam and Bihar, faced floods, drought was declared in Maharashtra, while others like Rajasthan, Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu are facing drought-like situations. Even India’s cities have not been spared by these climate impacts. The Reserve Bank of India has warned that extreme heat and humidity could put up to 4.5% of India’s GDP at risk by 2030 through lost labour hours. While these disasters differ in geography and hazard, together they underscore a common reality. Climate change is no longer a future environmental challenge. It is reshaping India’s economy, infrastructure and development in real time. At the same time, the Indian government has been taking steps towards adapting to these challenges. Six of the nine missions under the National Action Plan on Climate Change focus on adaptation, and 34 states and Union Territories have prepared State Action Plans on Climate Change. The latest Economic Survey tabled in January, classifies spending equal to 5.6% of GDP in 2021–22 as “adaptation and resilience-related”, up from 3.7% in 2015–16. While these investments and interventions are necessary, some fundamental questions receive far less attention: adaptation for whom and how? And who gets to make these decisions? These questions become particularly important as India prepares its first National Adaptation Plan (NAP), a roadmap that will shape public investment in climate resilience over the coming decades. This makes it worth examining how India should adapt to climate change and which…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.title: Protests over dam heat up as crackdown on activists continues
item.dc:creator: Simrin Sirur
item.author: Kundan Pandey
item.topic-tags: Activism, Dams, Hydroelectric power, and Rivers
item.description:
- Protests against the 11,000 MW Siang Upper Multipurpose Project in Arunachal Pradesh turned violent on September 30, with an MLA’s house attacked and vehicles allegedly set on fire.
- Activists opposing the dam face a growing crackdown, including a CBI case under FCRA, police summons, and restrictions on local news pages.
- The state calls the dam a “national project” to counter China’s Medog dam, but residents question the claim and the risks in a high-seismic zone.
item.content:encoded: Protests against the Siang Upper Multipurpose Project (SUMP) in Arunachal Pradesh have turned violent after more than a year of peaceful demonstrations. On October 4, protesters resisting the project  were allegedly lathi charged by police and paramilitary forces in Uggeng village. The police action comes days after protesters attacked an MLA’s house and allegedly set vehicles on fire during a scheduled visit to the region by Chief Minister Pema Khandu. Residents of the Siang and Upper Siang districts have consistently opposed the 11,000 megawatt dam project and blocked all efforts to carry out a Pre-Feasibility Report study (PFR) to determine its viability. Khandu planned to meet with residents of the area reportedly to have a dialogue about the project, and persuade them to allow feasibility studies to be carried out in the area. “People don’t want the PFR to take place because they don’t want the dam at all,” said Christina Pangam, a resident of Yingkiong and a local news reporter. Protests intensified on September 14 when the state government deployed hundreds of police and paramilitary forces to the villages of Uggeng and Komkar — among the three proposed sites of the dam. Residents blocked roads into the area to prevent the PFR from taking place. “There has been a lot of misinformation that has been creating anxiety about the PFR going through,” said Pangam. In June, Khandu said the government had obtained support to carry out the PFR from 110 families after signing a memorandum with them. According to…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.title: Climate change may increase the ibisbill’s habitat range, but other pressures loom
item.dc:creator: Hirra Azmat
item.author: Priyanka Shankar
item.topic-tags: Biodiversity, Birds, Climate Change, Conservation, Ecology, Forests, Himalayas, Impacts of Climate Change, Mountains, Rivers, and Wildlife
item.description:
- A new study finds that mean annual temperature is the most important climatic factor influencing the distribution of the elusive ibisbill within the Kashmir and Ladakh Himalayas.
- Future climate projections indicate an expansion in the ibisbill’s habitat range, particularly along mid-elevation river corridors.
- However, human activities such as boulder mining, plastic and garbage pollution, also add pressures on the ibisbill’s habitat.
item.content:encoded: The ibisbill (Ibidorhyncha struthersii), an elusive bird confined to the boulder-strewn mountain rivers of the Himalayas, has long remained one of the region’s least-studied species. Researchers have now produced the first detailed climate-based assessment of the bird in North-Western Himalayas, identifying where its suitable climatic conditions exist today and how they may shift under future warming. Listed as least concern in the IUCN red list, the ibisbill occurs across the Himalayas and the Tibetan Plateau. However, it  remains one of the most elusive riverine birds in the Himalayan region, restricted to specific habitats and with no conclusive population estimate from India, says Ankita Sinha, a wildlife biologist and researcher at Senckenberg Biodiversity and Climate Research Center, Frankfurt. “Because of their limited sightings and ranges restricted to remote uninhabited areas, knowledge on their ecology and behaviour is limited,” she says. The ibisbill is a high-altitude bird restricted to fast-flowing mountain rivers with gravel bars and often braided rivers. Image by Khursheed Ahmad. These specialist birds are restricted to fast-flowing high-altitude rivers, particularly ones with gravel bars and ones that are braided. Their long, curved bills are adapted to feeding between stones and under gravel, where they mainly feed on aquatic insects, larvae and other invertebrates. They also nest directly on gravel bars, making them highly dependent on intact river habitats. Its habitat, particularly near the towns and valleys, is also occupied by people, shares Asad Rahmani, an ornithologist and the former director of Bombay Natural History Society. item.title: Unclear records leave villages in limbo over irrigation project displacement
item.dc:creator: Ayushi Sharma
item.author: Kundan Pandey
item.reporting-project: Clean Energy and Flood and drought
item.description:
- Polavaram Irrigation Project on Godavari river leaves villages in the neighbouring state Chhattisgarh in fear about displacement, because of uncertainty about the project’s submergence area.
- Different government records cite different numbers of potentially affected villages in Chhattisgarh, leaving residents unclear about their residence.
- The Polavaram project aims to create irrigation potential for 2.91 lakh hectares, generate 960 MW of hydropower, supply drinking water to about 28 lakh people.
item.content:encoded: Manglu Dorla’s house stands where the forest opens into the Sabari river in Konta, a village in the Sukma district of southern Chhattisgarh. Dorla’s family has farmed the land for generations. The forest supplies the fuel, fodder, and food. Now, he fears that he may be forced to abandon his home, along with other residents of the village. This fear stems from a dam being built more than a hundred kilometres downstream on the Godavari river in Andhra Pradesh. Will that project affect his village? He and other residents of Konta are unsure. “None of us wants to leave our home,” Dorla said. The Polavaram Irrigation Project (PIP), is located on the Godavari river near Ramanayyapeta in Polavaram mandal, Andhra Pradesh. It is about 42 kilometres upstream of the Sir Arthur Cotton Barrage, where the river emerges from the Eastern Ghats and enters the coastal plains of Andhra Pradesh. The elevation of the structure is 45.72 metres or 150 feet. Sabari, a tributary of the Godavari river, originates in the Eastern Ghats in Odisha, forms part of the boundary between Odisha and Chhattisgarh, and later enters Andhra Pradesh before joining the Godavari. The Polavaram project The Polavaram Irrigation Project’s construction began in 2004, after decades of interstate negotiation stretching back to a 1980 agreement signed when today’s Chhattisgarh was still part of Madhya Pradesh. item.title: Maharashtra formally recognises women farmers regardless of land ownership [Commentary]
item.dc:creator: Soumya Swaminathan
item.author: Aditi Tandon
item.topic-tags: Agriculture, Climate Change, Climate Change Adaptation, Environmental Law, Environmental Politics, Food, and Organic Farming
item.description:
- Women have increasingly taken up the role of managing and maintaining the agricultural lands, often with more responsibility but without a corresponding rise in control, assets or decision-making power.
- Maharashtra’s Women Farmer’s Empowerment Act 2026 is a powerful example of what can happen when political will and a clear understanding of why empowering women matters, writes the author of this commentary.
- Under the Act, women engaged in agriculture or allied activities will formally be recognised as farmers, even when they do not own the land. This will open doors for many women who sow, tend, harvest and manage our agri-foods systems but are often left out of the formal definition of a farmer.
- The views in this commentary are those of the author.
item.content:encoded: On October 2, Maharashtra is set to begin issuing the Women Farmers Certificates (WFCs) under the newly enacted Women Farmer’s Empowerment Act 2026. The certificates will formally recognise women engaged in agriculture or allied activities as farmers, even when they do not own the land. The WFC will open doors for lakhs of women who sow, tend, harvest and manage our agri-foods systems, as well as livestock, poultry and fisheries, but are often left out of the formal definition of a farmer. Maharashtra has shown political will and a clear sense of urgency in bringing women farmers’ needs into the spotlight and leading by example. Feminisation of agriculture  We have been witnessing feminisation of agriculture for some time now. As men move to non-farm jobs, women have increasingly taken up the role of managing and maintaining the agricultural lands. But this has often meant more responsibility without a corresponding rise in control, assets or decision-making power. Without land titles, they also struggle to access critical resources such as credit, water, technology and extension services, reducing them to labourers in a sector they largely sustain. Nationally, women make up close to 60% of the agricultural workforce as reported by the Periodic Labour Force Survey and shared by the Union Minister of State for Agriculture, Ramnath Thakur recently in Parliament, but they hold less than 15% of land titles. In Maharashtra, 82% of the rural female workforce is engaged in agriculture, yet women hold only about 15.5% of operational farmland. item.title: Legal system fails to keep pace with India’s growing exotic pet industry
item.dc:creator: Arathi Menon
item.author: Aditi Tandon
item.topic-tags: Animals, Biodiversity, Birds, Environmental Law, Law Enforcement, Pet Trade, Primates, Reptiles, Wildlife, Wildlife Protection Act, Wildlife Trade, Wildlife Trafficking, and Zoos
item.description:
- India has strengthened its legal framework to regulate the exotic pet trade, but implementation remains fragmented.
- The 2020 Voluntary Disclosure Scheme saw more than 40,000 people declare non-native exotic pets, but experts point to limited follow-up action.
- Poor regulation, online trafficking and links to other illegal trade is compounded by weak systems for surrendered and seized animals.
item.content:encoded: This is Part 4 of a series on exotic pet trade. The series looks at the health impacts, legal challenges and the ecological consequences of keeping exotic wild animals as pets. Part 1 explores how the trade enables zoonoses; Part 2 observes how India is emerging as a link in the global primate trade; and Part 3 raises the animal welfare and ecological concerns of abandoned or escaped pets. Jose Louies has witnessed India’s wildlife pet trade scene change dramatically over the last decade and a half. The CEO of the non-profit Wildlife Trust of India (WTI), he calls himself an “old hand in the business”, having relentlessly tracked the trade over the last two decades. In the early years of the millennium, Louies recalls, colourful birds and large parrots such as sulphur-crested cockatoos and macaws were mainly seen in circuses. “Even zoos had very few exotic animals,” he says. Some of the ultra-rich may have kept a parrot or two in their farmhouses, while pet markets at Jama Masjid, Crawford Market in Mumbai and markets in Kolkata had budgerigars, cockatoos and other small exotic birds. “The markets were quite discreet and there were hardly any exotic mammals,” Louies says. Native species such as Alexandrine parakeets and Indian hill myna were seen in illegal markets, while goldfish were mostly preferred as pets. Forest departments and organisations such as PETA and People for Animals (PFA) were also quite active in monitoring or cracking down on illegal trade, he recalls. item.content:encoded: Species File: Exploring India’s biodiversity, one species at a time. Flying thousands of kilometres circumventing the mighty Himalayas, harriers arrive in India’s grasslands around July every year, when winter sets in across their breeding grounds in Central Asia and Russia. Mated pairs perform a suave mid-air food pass, with the male dropping prey for the female to catch during flight. They hunt by the day, circling low and in zigzag patterns to find small mammals, birds, reptiles, and insects. In addition to controlling their prey populations, a recent study found that two harrier species — the pallid and Montagu’s harriers — are surprisingly also grassland gardeners; they consume seeds carried inside their prey’s gut and later expel them unharmed. Of the 16 harrier species found worldwide, six visit India — Montagu’s, pallid, hen, pied, and the Eurasian (western) and eastern marsh harriers. Unusually for raptors, they nest on the ground, and roost communally in large numbers with other harrier species — the world’s largest such roost documented so far was at Velavadar National Park, Gujarat. Most harrier species are listed as least concern by the IUCN, except the pallid harrier, which is near threatened due to a global population decline. In India, harriers receive the highest legal protection under Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. item.content:encoded: A May 2026 study describes a new species of toad (Duttaphyrnus phawngpui sp. nov.) from Phawngpui National Park, located in southeastern Mizoram along the border with Myanmar. Researchers studied two individuals found at the hilltops. The species was named after Phawngpui, Mizoram’s highest mountain peak at 2,157 metres above sea level. True toads of the Duttaphyrnus genus occur as many species in varied habitats in South and Southeast Asia — often even in polluted areas. However, the newly described species and its closest relatives, D. stuarti, D. chandai and D. dhara, are largely restricted to the higher ranges of the eastern Himalayas, according to Jayaditya Purkayastha, a co-author of the study. Morphological and DNA analyses of the two specimens collected helped identify distinctions from the previously known species. Researchers encountered D. phawngpui sp. nov. individuals among leaf litter on the forest floor along the edge of a trail leading to the summit of Phawngpui at above 2,000 masl. The area was abundant in dense ground cover in the form of shrubbery as well as bamboo patches, and had relatively low human disturbance, hinting at the toad’s preferred ecosystem features. D. phawngpui and its relatives are facing the immediate threat of habitat loss, as the tops of mountains (sky islands) that offer ideal conditions, shrink in size. “They are habitat specific, not generalists, meaning they can only survive in certain conditions. D. phawngpui is a ground dwelling frog that requires grassy patches, high humidity and forest streams, especially for breeding,” says…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.title: India’s coking coal push needs a methane plan [Commentary]
item.dc:creator: Purva JainSaumya Nautiyal
item.author: Kundan Pandey
item.topic-tags: Carbon emissions, Clean Energy, Climate Change, Coal, Energy, Environment, Fossil Fuels, Greenhouse Gas Emissions, Industry, Pollution, Sustainability, Technology, and Villages
item.description:
- India’s plan to ramp up coking coal mining could increase methane emissions faster as mines go deeper into gassier seams.
- A few mines, mostly in Jharkhand, account for most of these emissions, so targeted action and early checks can avoid decades of lock-in.
- Much of this methane can be abated reasonably, and capturing it for use can even pay for itself.
- The views in this commentary are those of the authors.
item.content:encoded: India is preparing to double its coking coal output by 2030, especially to meet its steel manufacturing needs. While carbon emissions from coal use are well known, coal mining also produces methane emissions, which warrant early attention. If monitoring and abatement measures are not incorporated at the planning stage, it could lock in higher emissions in mining operations for decades. Methane is a potent greenhouse gas and is formed in coal mines during the coalification process. It remains trapped within the coal seam and is released when mining disturbs or exposes the seam to the atmosphere. These emissions are called coal mine methane (CMM) and occur during multiple stages of the mining cycle, including extraction, drainage, and ventilation, as well as post-mining activities such as coal processing, storage, and transport. Coking coal mining is particularly methane-intensive, with around 50% higher methane intensity than non-coking coal. When heated in the absence of air, coking coal converts into coke: a strong, porous material, low in ash and moisture and free of volatile matter. Coke’s use as a fuel and a reducing agent in steel production sets it apart from non-coking coal, which is primarily used for energy generation. Why is India planning for more coking coal? In the absence of good-quality domestically produced coking coal, India imports around 90% of the coking coal required by its steel sector, which needs low ash and sulphur content and caking properties.
